The papers develops a way to estimate gradients of functions approximated using ensembles of regression trees.
The authors present an intuitive algorithm that is practically effective and demonstrate that the proposed method can consistently recover gradients.

Several referees raised concerns about the gap between practice and the assumptions on which the theory rests. In particular, concern was raised over the use of data-dependent splits in practice but midpoint splits in theory. I do not view this gap as specifically disqualifying and would like to thank the authors for a productive discussion around this point. I am encouraged that they see a path towards establishing similar theoretical results under weaker assumptions. 

I strongly encourage the authors to include a short remark in a revised version of the manuscript that acknowledges this gap and a few sentences in the discussion about how future work may bridge this gap. In doing so, please be sure to cite the additional papers referenced in the rebuttals. They should, of course, additionally follow through on the minor changes and clarifications raised by the referees and addressed in the discussion period (e.g., clarifying the midpoint split assumption in Assumption 1.3, editing captions for Figures 9-12, fixing typos and making sure notation is defined precisely, etc.)

Many thanks again to reviewers for their thoughtful reviews! 

We were very pleased to hear that the opinions on the article were mostly positive, and are grateful for the additional clarity and presentation improvements made possible by our interactions. 

We hope that the reviewers agree that our simple but powerful method for bringing gradients to regression trees will have important consequences both for interpretability of regression trees and for bringing regression trees more fully into the scientific machine learning space. 

We'd like to now make a closing comment to each reviewer.

**ERhD**: Thanks for all your careful feedback, and especially engaging with us on the statistical presentation of results and the important midpoint assumption. As we wrote below, this is a common simplifying assumption made in the regression tree literature, and we have for the AC's convenience reproduced a non-exhaustive list of some recent papers in top ML confs using this assumption. 

**oJvh**: Thanks so much for your careful critical attention to our article. We regret that we were not able to discuss these points in the discussion period but we still benefited from your feedback. 

**XQAw**: Thanks for your careful attention to our proofs, and for pushing us to expand our pointwise convergence to a uniform one, which indeed held essentially under our existing assumption and proof strategy. 

**UaXM**: Thanks for pushing us to better explain our assumptions and for the literature suggestions. We think this resulted in a better exposition of our method. 

Of course each review had much more to say but we simply list some highlights here.

--

We just want to quickly clarify: **we are happy with the midpoint split assumption for trees, and are not planning on removing it**. This is a common simplifying assumption made in the regression tree literature (looking very briefly, it's made by for example Kazemitabar et al '17 Neurips), particularly in papers whose contribution is not primarily theoretical, but methodological, such as this one. When we said "we hope to provide the body of this proof before the end of the discussion period on 6 August", we mean one which provides uniform rather than pointwise convergence under the existing assumptions. 

Thanks for suggesting the ANOVA. This is a reasonable choice, too. Note, however, that common ANOVAs assume homoskedasticity across the different methods, something which our method-specific confidence intervals avoid. References:
Kazemitabar, Jalil, et al. "Variable importance using decision trees." Advances in neural information processing systems 30 (2017).

I have read all the reviews, and the rebuttal for each one.

* I note the point made by reviewer XQAw that "the splitting threshold is data dependent, and that that one cannot directly claim the square-root rate from the CLT." The proof provided in Appendix A only applies to a "splitting point at the midpoint of the cell" (see rebuttal to reviewer UaXM). The authors say in their rebuttal to XQAw that "we hope to provide the body of this proof before the end of the discussion period on 6 August". There is clearly a major problem with the paper here; I will reserve my judgement until if/when a revised proof is provided, and if the referees (esp XQAw) find this to be valid.

* Re: paired testing. Consider a repeated measures (or within-subjects) 2-way ANOVA model $y_{ij} = \mu + \alpha_i + \beta_j + \epsilon_{ij}$, where $\alpha_i$ is the fixed effect of method $i$, and $\beta_j$ is a random effect, e.g. from test example $j$. Then the paired difference on example j for algorithms i and k is $d_j =
\alpha_i - \alpha_k + \epsilon_{ij} - \epsilon_{kj}$, in other words the "example effect" $\beta_j$ is removed by this paired difference. Hence the variance associated with $\beta_j$ is removed, compared to the error bars for condition $i$.

Thanks very much for your detailed comments on and positive assessment of our article; we are quite grateful for your time. 

Below, we respond in detail to all the points you brought up (shown in italics) and to your questions.

**Weaknesses**

- *I am not sure why the “2” in the central equation...*: Great question: speaking at an intuitive level, it is because the mean terms are averages over the whole node, whereas in the denominator we have the extremes of the nodes. We've added this intuition to that section.
- *Figure 2 is not properly referenced...*: Thanks for pointing out the lack of Figure 2 reference; we now refer to it in the introduction.
- *Figure 3 should be made bigger...*: We agree that Figure 3 is a bit cramped. We would use the additional space in the camera-ready version to enlarge it and place it after the notation introduction.
- *The theorems in Section 4 require assumptions which are only given in the Appendix...*: Responding to your question below has made us realize that we did a poor job discussing the implications of the assumptions. We have given some discussion in response to that question below, which we would include in a camera-ready version. 
- *Section 5.2 should reference to Appendix B.1 ...*: Yes great point, we have added reference to Appendix B to Section 5.2
- *I was not able to assess the supplementary material...*: It is regretful that you were not able to access the supplementary material; we have just confirmed that we can download it and extract it from OpenReview on our Windows device successfully. It consists simply of Python code which reproduces every figure in the article. 
- *There are also minor grammatical, spelling and consistency issues*: We did indeed notice some grammatical issues etc when reviewing the article; we have now fixed several of these issues. Thank you for bringing this to our attention.

**Questions**

1. Thanks for this interesting question. In answering it, we have realized that our discussion of assumptions in the article was woefully inadequate, and would add some of the following discussion to the body of a camera-ready paper. The most important deviation of our theoretical assumptions from the typical deployment of tree-based methods in practice is the splitting behavior, namely Assumption 1.3. This states that splits alternate between variables, and it should also state that the splits are made at the midpoint of the cell (thanks to Reviewer XQAw for leading us to this omission). In practice, which variable is to be split, as well as the split location, depends on the data. However, this aspect may have a limited impact on our conclusions, because the fact that we will in practice split more often along impactful variables means that we are likely to build more precise estimates for larger elements of the gradient. We suspect, however, that the situation is actually improved for gradient estimates in practical algorithms relative to our simplified model. Of course, this discussion is at an intuitive level and a more rigorous mathematical examination would be interesting as future work. Assumption 1.1, which says that the predictors have a continuous distribution, may not be satisfied for certain data generating mechanisms which produce predictor variables only in certain submanifolds of the input space. In these circumstances, gradient estimation will of course be unreliable in locations of the input space in which we do not have data (as would be the case for function value estimation itself). Assumption 1.2, that the error converges at the square root rate, will generally be satisfied for iid data, but may be violated in the case of data with very strong spatiotemporal correlation which could trick the regression tree into modeling the error instead of the function. Most ML algorithms will suffer in this situation. Assumption 1.4, of a continuously differentiable function, holds for some of our case studies (namely 5.3, 5.4, 5.5) but not others (5.1 and potentially some of 5.2). We have demonstrated empirically that the gradient estimates are still useful without differentiability assumptions, but it is in our view interesting future work to study its behavior in this setting mathematically, which would require a completely different approach as series expansions would no longer be appropriate. 

2. Thanks for pointing us to this fascinating article which compares BShap to IG and other Shapley-derived sensitivity metrics. One clear difference between BShap and our proposed method is the requirement for the specification of a baseline value for BShap, much as is required for IG. Another is the way in which the methods compare function values: in BShap, a given feature is changed from fully at the baseline to fully at a given “explicand” (to use Sundararajan and Najmi’s term), while for the TBGE, the change becomes increasingly small as the tree depth grows. However, there are also similarities, as Sundararajan and Najmi  show that BShap satisfies linearity in the sense that the BShap value for a function f = h + g is the sum of the BShaps for h and g, a property of course shared by the gradient as well. We would add some of this discussion to the related work section of a camera-ready paper.

3. We agree that the numerical experiments indicate that the performance is greatest in smaller trees, and we also noticed this in informal preliminary experiments. On the one hand, this is surprising because we only expect the TBGE to give a good gradient estimate if the tree is deep. But on the other hand, the potential for a data transformation to impact the accuracy of a tree is greatest if its depth is limited. It seems that this second factor is outweighing the first. We view as important future work a study determining the mathematical behavior of the TBGE in trees of finite depth. Though it may not converge to the gradient, it may nevertheless encode important information about the function. We have added some of this discussion to the conclusions and future work sections.

Thanks very much for your positive review and for taking the time to carefully review our article. We respond in detail to all the points you brought up (shown in italics) and to your questions below. 


**Main Points**

- *Title*: It’s true that the current title is not a classical staid academic title. But there is something to be said about titles which stimulate the prospective reader’s curiosity. Imagine if Vaswani et al had named their article “Attention mechanisms subsume other neural architectures on natural language tasks” rather than "Attention is all you need"...
- *Eq 3: Mus not defined*. While we did define these in the first sentence of Section 3.1, we should have also included them in our notation illustration Figure 3 and now do so.
- *Sec 5.1*: Thanks for pointing out that $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{x}^* $ are not defined in our IG experiment; this was an omission on our part and we have rectified this. You were correct in your assumption that $\mathbf{x}$ is the current digit. $\mathbf{x}^*$ is set as the all black image, i.e. with all entries equal to 0. You are correct that gradients are not well defined on this application. Nevertheless, the TBGE for any finite sample is, and in numerical experiments appears to behave reasonably.
- *Sec 5.2*: Thanks for pointing out that we forgot to mention our confidence level; it is 95%. For the rest, please see below in the “Questions” section.
- *Sec 5.3*: good point, we have moved that function’s definition to Section 5.2.

**Other**

- Thanks for pointing out our citation inconsistencies; we have gone through the text to rectify this. Apologies for any inconvenience this caused in reading.
- *line 112*: thanks for pointing out this error which we have resolved.
- “a” is simply the name of the argument for the function h; we now state as much.
- Good catch regarding “principal component”; we’ve changed this.
- We see what you mean regarding Figures 9-12 and have updated the caption information to be more informative.

**Questions**

- *Table 1*: Thanks for this question. 

First, it's worth mentioning that at the fundamental level of philosophy of frequentist statistics, there is no special advantage to doing a paired test relative to comparing confidence interval overlap, and each can be calibrated to have an arbitrary type I error rate. In the opinion of the statistician currently writing, it is an accident of history that paired tests are viewed as the “correct” procedure. Flow-charts can be a good starting point for research teams without access to statistical expertise, but ultimately determining the right statistical procedure for an analysis is a subjective decision which must be made in light of all domain and analytic information as well as the constraints of the medium in which the results will be presented. 

We can think of two ways to deploy a paired test. In the first way, we would compare all methods to each other method, which would make for a more cluttered table, since we would have to assess significance of each test relative to each other test.
In the second way, we would compare only the best performing method to the other methods. 
But this is not the hypothesis that is being assessed by the paired tests: it doesn't account for the randomness inherent in which method was the "best" performing one.
We would need to account for this using a more sophisticated statistical procedure. 
On the other hand, confidence intervals are well understood and easy to present in this context. Hence our decision to go with them. 
But ultimately, we are here deciding between flavors of ice cream (to use the classical example from moral philosophy), and there is no right answer.

We now state this explicitly in the figure caption.

Thanks so much for taking the time to carefully consider our work. We greatly appreciate it.

We'll now address the comments you made under "Weaknesses" and your questions. 

**Regarding Weaknesses**

Thanks very much for taking the time to think critically about our article. However, after careful consideration, we have found that we disagree with most of your weakness assessments. 

In each bullet, the italics indicate what we are responding to, and the standard text is our response.

- *Limited scope of Applications*: You are commenting on the scope of our mathematical results, not of our applications. In fact, many of our empirical results are on messy, real world applications, and provide empirical evidence that the method can perform well in this setting. 
- *Questionable Fundamental Assumption*: We’d like to challenge the frame of this assertion; we are in fact suggesting that trees are useful on additional classes of problems than they are typically selected for, including for friendly functions. 
- *Weak Empirical Results*: The strength of the result depends on the method used, with weaker results for individual trees and stronger ones for Random Forests. In practice, trees are commonly used within ensembling methods. On the random forest, our method offers significant improvement on 6/8 test problems, including halving the error on the popular keggu problem. Additionally, this criticism considers only 1 of 5 empirical applications. 

*Incomplete Evaluation*

- *Incomplete Evaluation (1) - other methods*: The methods you’ve mentioned are for the importance of individual variables, not linear combinations of variables, and hence cannot be used to perform a linear rotation of the space like active subspaces or PCA. Since trees are invariant to scaling individual features, it is not clear how to include these methods in our experiments. 
- *Incomplete Evaluation (2) - Limited analysis*: Appendix C.1 shows how the method can fail if the tree depth is small relative to the function complexity. 
- *Incomplete Evaluation (3) - Missing evaluation on truly discontinuous functions*: Section 5.1 is on MNIST classification and Appendix C.5 consider classification versions of all our datasets, which manifests as a discontinuous function. The proposed method still seems to perform well. 

*Presentation Issues*

- *Presentation Issues (1) - Notation*: We agree that the idea is much more intuitive than the notation. Believe it or not, the notation used to be even more burdensome, and we have spent much time thinking how to make it simpler, including providing figure 3 which illustrates all aspects of our notation. We welcome any specific advice for improved notation.
- *Presentation Issues (2) - Some claims are overstated (e.g., "first such linear sensitivity metric for trees")*:  Of course, we acknowledge in the introduction that linear dimension reduction in general has been used in conjunction with trees, but to the best of our knowledge, the tree structure itself has not previously contributed to this dimension reduction. While we did perform a thorough literature review, it is completely possible that we have missed a previous linear sensitivity metric for trees, and in this event we would be very grateful if you could provide us a specific example of one.
- *Presentation Issues (3) - The connection between gradient quality and tree depth could be made more explicit*: Theorem 4.1 gives a bound on the gradient error in terms of the number of splits in the tree. Under the assumption of uniform splitting, this is linearly related to the depth. 

--

- *Theoretical Limitations The convergence rate… may be slow in practice*: We agree that there is always room for additional theoretical analysis about this method. However, our empirical studies demonstrate that the method does indeed work in practice.

**Response to Questions**
- Q: *Can you better characterize when your gradient estimates are reliable?*
- A: We could envision interesting future work which uses a statistical test of linearity as is classically done in, e.g. ANOVAs combined with an estimate of the error variance to produce a bound on gradient quality. In the present work, we assessed reliability teleologically using out of sample prediction error. 

--

- Q: *What happens on discontinuous functions where trees typically excel?*
- A: From an applications perspective, we found that the method yielded useful results on a classification problem, which is of course discontinuous. From a mathematical perspective, using discontinuous functions complicates the analysis significantly, and would necessitate a different approach, since ours is based on Taylor’s theorem and thus first order differentiability. We view this as important future work.

--

- Q:  *Consider providing failure cases or bounds on estimation quality.*
- A: Re failure cases: Figure 9 of the Appendix’s left column shows how a tree of insufficient depth fails to provide good gradient estimates even in large sample sizes. Re: estimation quality bounds: Theorem 4.1 provides an asymptotic bound on estimation quality. We view the development of finite sample bounds as interesting future work. 

--

- Q: *How do your gradient estimates compare to true gradients on known smooth functions? Can you show convergence behavior as tree depth increases?*
- A: Answering this question is the purpose of Appendix section C.1.

--

- Q: *What depth and sample size requirements are needed for reliable gradient estimation in different dimensions? Can you provide practical guidance for practitioners?*
- A: Theorem 4.1 provides rates for the relative values of those quantities from an asymptotic perspective. As we mentioned in response to your first question, we could envision an interesting future approach which can provide this practical guidance by providing a finite sample bound of gradient error. But rather than constructing a tree guaranteed to achieve a particular gradient estimation error, we rather view practitioners taking the trees they are already using and applying the TBGE to it to see what it can tell them about their existing analyses.

--

- Q: *How does TBAS compare to established tree interpretability methods like SHAP values or permutation importance?*
- A: As a linear dimension reduction method, it extends the variable-specific importance of SHAP and permutation to determining important linear subspaces. 

--

- Q: *How does the method perform with categorical variables, missing data, or truly non-smooth functions that motivate tree usage?*
- A: It’s not immediately obvious how this method would be applied to categorical variables. One clear option for addressing missing data would be to combine this method with multiple imputation. Though our mathematical results do not extend to nonsmooth functions, our empirical results, including on the MNIST classification, demonstrated useful behavior on discontinuous functions.


Thanks again for taking the time to carefully consider our work, and we look forward to having a great discussion during the rebuttal period.

summary.value: This paper introduces a method for estimating gradients from regression trees by computing finite differences between adjacent nodes in the tree structure. The authors propose using these gradient estimates to enable gradient-based interpretability techniques for tree models, specifically focusing on Active Subspace methods and Integrated Gradients. The key insight is that the difference in mean responses between left and right splits, normalized by node width, approximates partial derivatives. The paper demonstrates applications including tree-based active subspace estimation (TBAS), tree-based integrated gradients (TBIG), and shows these can improve predictive performance and provide model interpretation.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
### Strengths
- The core idea of extracting gradient information from tree structures is genuinely innovative and opens up new possibilities for tree-based interpretability.
- The paper provides asymptotic analysis (Theorems 4.1, 4.2) establishing consistency of the gradient estimators under reasonable assumptions.
- The method enables tree models to leverage existing gradient-based tools from other ML domains, potentially bridging interpretability techniques across model classes.
- The gradient estimation can be computed in a single tree traversal, making it computationally attractive.
- The evaluation covers multiple applications (active subspace estimation, integrated gradients, predictive improvement) across various datasets.

### Weaknesses
- Limited Scope of Application: The method requires "sufficiently deep" trees on "well-behaved, differentiable functions." This significantly restricts its applicability since trees are often valued precisely for handling discontinuous or pathological data.
- Questionable Fundamental Assumption: The paper's premise that regression trees can meaningfully approximate gradients of smooth functions contradicts why trees are typically chosen - their ability to handle non-smooth, discontinuous relationships.
- Weak Empirical Results: Table 1 shows modest improvements that often fall within confidence intervals. The benefits don't strongly justify the additional complexity.
- Incomplete Evaluation:
- - No comparison to established tree interpretability methods (SHAP, permutation importance)
- - Limited analysis of when the method fails or produces poor gradient estimates
- - Missing evaluation on truly discontinuous functions
- Presentation Issues:
- - Heavy notation makes the core simple idea unnecessarily complex
- - Some claims are overstated (e.g., "first such linear sensitivity metric for trees")
- - The connection between gradient quality and tree depth could be made more explicit

- Theoretical Limitations: The convergence rate of \sqrt(P N^(-1) log N) may be slow in practice, and the assumptions (differentiability, sufficient depth) are quite restrictive.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strength: The overall idea is an important extension of widely used regression tree models. The proposed algorithm is simple and intuitive. The authors have demonstrated the usefulness of this idea with a couple of applications. The paper is well-written -- I enjoy reading it a lot. 

Weakness: The theoretical guarantees are not very satisfactory. 
Looking into Assumption 1 in the supplementary material, it seems that Theorem 4.1 relies on an assumption that the mean of f(x) in a give leaf converges at square-root rate. This assumption itself need to be proved for many tree-fitting algorithms. For example, if one use CART to fit the tree, then the splitting threshold itself will be data-dependent, and one cannot directly claim the square-root rate from CLT.

questions.value:

However, in practice, when trees are used in boosting or random forest, each individual tree would usually not be very deep. summary.value: This paper proposes a simple method to estimate the gradient of a target function in a piecewise-constant regression tree, as per Algorithm 1. This is used to approximate the Integrated Gradient and Active Subspace Method as per sec 2.3. A variety of experiments indicates the utility of this method for regression trees.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Title: "Regression Trees Know Calculus" is a rather provocative title, attributing self-awareness ("know") to regression trees. A  more academic title would be something like "Obtaining and Exploiting Gradient Information from Regression Trees".

Eq 3: \mu^r_i and \mu^l_i have not been defined!

Sec 4: I did not check the proofs in detail (Appendix A).

Sec 5.1 (IG): Re Fig 4. IG requires two points x and x^*. It is not explained what these are in your experiments. I guess x is the current digit (e.g. the 0 in left most panel), but what is x^*?
Lacking this information I do not find Fig 4 useful. Also the gradient is estimated at all pixels, not just the black ones (anyway, as I recall MNIST pixel values are real-valued). Why are the values only shown for the black pixels, or are the other values near 0? It would be better to show the IG values per pixel without the digit in the background.

Also presumably this target function has only 2 values (e.g. +1/-1 for the two classes) -- so is a gradient actually well defined here?

Sec 5.2 Table 1. I appreciate the efforts to indicate similar performance, as per the caption "bold indicates confidence interval overlaps with the lowest confidence interval". But confidence interval at what level (alpha?). Also, bear in mind that you are using the same test set so can do *paired comparisons*. Overall Table 1 suggests that TBAS improves over the identity and PCA rotations. Please also refer to Appendix B.1 and Fig 8 from the main text, as additional information is provided there.

More broadly, Rainio, O., Teuho, J. & Klen, R., Evaluation metrics and statistical tests for machine learning. Sci Rep 14, 6086 (2024). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-56706-x provides a useful flowchart (Fig 3) and sttaistical tests for the comparison of different methods. 

Sec 5.3: Please explain what the function you are estimating is in the main text. (It is given in B.2). Also define how you compute the "active subspace error" (perhaps angle in radians, cosine of angle??)

* Other points

Please distinguish between textual and paranthetical citations
properly. e.g. l 103 should be (Constantine, 2015) not as written, and
there are many other examples.  I recommend natbib (e.g. \citet, \citep)
for doing this.

l 112 easy-to-compute

l 169: \bold{a} is undefined. And why change notation from x to z?

l 286: second principal component -> second active subspace component?

Fig 9. This figure is not comprehensible without the text in sec C.1. The graphics and caption together should *explain* the figure, so you need to explain what the colour coding means (angle between true and
estimated gradient)in the figure. Check other figures similarly. 

Quality: Good. Although I did not check the asymptotic analysis results in detail (sec 4), I find these results credible. The experiments are quite well done, but see comments above re significance of differences
in Table 1.

Clarity: Good. I found the paper quite well written, except for a few gaps highlighted above.

Significance: Good: Despite the high profile of (deep) neural networks, it is true that decision tree methods are heavily used in data science applications, and thus advancements for regression trees could have
significant impact.  To me the strongest result in the experiments is Table 1, and the improvements made by TBAS rotation.

Originality: Good: AFAIK there has not been prior work on estimating derivatives in regression trees. Alg 1 is almost embarassingly simple -- it is probably what you would come up with if someone forced
you to estimate a gradient from a piecewise-constant regression trees. But still, it seems not to have been done before, and to be useful, and there is an asymptotic analysis of its properties.

questions.value:
Table 1: Please comment on the issue of the significance of differences, given my comments above.

Sec 5.1: Please clarify how x^* is chosen in these experiments. Also in Fig 4, should there be IG values for all pixels?

Good answers to these questions would increase my overall score a bit.

final_justification.value:
I was positive about this paper initially, and remain so after the rebuttals and discussion phase.

Reviewer XQAw raised an important point that "the splitting threshold is data dependent, and that that one cannot directly claim the square-root rate from the CLT." The authors responded that their
midpoint split assumption they use for the proof is very common in the literature for trees (and gave examples). They clarified that they would enhance the discussion of the assumptions etc in the final
paper.  I am satisfied by this.

The authors share with me a concern about the statistical significance of differences in performance, e.g. for Table 1. Another thought on this is that they might consider the frequentist correlated t-test
discussed, e.g.,  in Benavoli et al (2017), which can handle correlations in results due to cross-validation. 
Benavoli, A., Corani, G., Demšar, J., and Zaffalon, M. (2017). Time for a Change: a Tutorial for Comparing Multiple Classifiers Through Bayesian Analysis. Journal of Machine Learning Research, 18(77):1–36.

summary.value: The paper suggests a method to estimate derivatives/gradients for sufficiently large regression trees. On this basis, estimators which transfer the integrated gradient method and the active subspace method from neural networks to regression trees are developed. The experiments show applicability for local explainability of model predictions and promising results in different settings related to the active subspace method, in particular regarding active subspace estimation.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Quality: From what I can tell, the submission seems technically sound, and proofs are provided for the theoretical results. I appreciate that a variety of applications/experiments was shown, and found especially the study on local explainability of model predictions on MNIST to be intriguing. The results regarding active subspace estimation are also convincing. It is clear from the experiments and the discussion that much effort was expended; substantial additional material is contained in the Appendix.

Clarity: I found the paper to be mostly clear overall. The introduction of the concepts/methods, including the ones from literature (integrated gradient, active subspace), is generally well done. However, there is also potential for improvement. I am not sure why the “2” in the central equation (3) is needed. Figure 2 is not properly referenced, only in the caption of Figure 3, even though it greatly helps to understand how the method works. Figure 3 should be made bigger and introduced a bit later; currently, it is almost impossible to analyze as it is so small, and most of the notation explained is not yet introduced at this point in the paper. The theorems in Section 4 require assumptions which are only given in the Appendix, and I suggest to at least give a hint of what these assumptions are in the main body of the paper. Section 5.2 should reference to Appendix B.1 where the datasets for Table 1 are introduced. In addition, I was not able to assess the supplementary material (when extracting, it consists of a single file without file ending). There are also minor grammatical, spelling and consistency issues (inconsistent capitalization, repeated introduction of abbreviations etc.) that should be rectified.

Significance: The introduction does a good job in clarifying the motivation of the work and the background highlights important related concepts/methods. I was well able to understand the rationale behind the paper and am convinced that a gradient approximation for regression trees can be of great value and can advance understanding in a meaningful way. I also find both the applicability for local explainability as well as for uncertainty quantification to be highly intriguing. I am unsure about the feasibility of the assumptions for the theorems in Section 4, however.

Originality: With its novel methods, the paper seeks to improve understanding of regression trees and enable additional applications for this method, which I find to be very interesting as it may prove to be complementary to research on neural networks. A lot of implications and potential for future work are highlighted in the paper. The overall reasoning for originality is convincing. While a brief discussion of SHAP is provided in the paper, I would be interested in an examination of the relation to BSHAP (Sundararajan & Najmi 2020).

Mukund Sundararajan, Amir Najmi (2020). Proceedings of the 37th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 119:9269-9278.

In sum, I found the paper to be a good read and wish the authors all the best for their work on this interesting topic.

questions.value:
1. As stated above, I am unsure about the feasibility of the assumptions for the (central!) theorems in Section 4 and the description/explaination is very brief. Could you elaborate whether they are typically fulfilled? Are there some clear conditions under which the assumptions are certain to be fulfilled? What is an example for not fulfilling the assumptions?
2. As stated above, I would be interested in an examination of the relation to BSHAP (Sundararajan & Najmi 2020). From my understanding, this work (amongst others) discusses how splits in tree-based models encode gradient-like behaviors, which is a similar form of local explainability as well. 
3. The advantage of TBAS over the competing approaches seems to diminish for higher depth of the regression tree (cf. Table 1). Is this true and what is the reason for it?

If these questions are addressed satisfactorily, I may increase my evaluation score.

final_justification.value:
The paper suggests an interesting novel idea and shows a variety of applications, with convincing and intriguing results. The authors have thoroughly discussed all weaknesses and questions I brought up and provided clear, sound indication how they intend to address the weaknesses and resolve the questions in a camera ready version, including some helpful clarifications.
I have also read the discussion regarding the proof of uniform convergence/the “splitting point at the midpoint of the cell” (which seem like two issues mixed up) and, regardless of outcome, do not think that this aspect is central to the paper and its main idea.
Thus, I overall keep my recommendation to accept the paper.

TLDR.value: Use differences between means in tree splits to estimate function derivatives; now we have gradient-based methods for trees.

abstract.value: Regression trees have emerged as a preeminent tool for solving real-world regression problems due to their ability to deal with nonlinearities, interaction effects and sharp discontinuities. In this article, we rather study regression trees applied to well-behaved, differentiable functions, and determine the relationship between node parameters and the local gradient of the function being approximated. We find a simple estimate of the gradient which can be efficiently computed using quantities exposed by popular tree learning libraries. This allows tools developed in the context of differentiable algorithms, like neural nets and Gaussian processes, to be deployed to tree-based models. To demonstrate this, we study measures of model sensitivity defined in terms of integro-differential quantities and demonstrate how to compute them for regression trees using the proposed gradient estimates. Quantitative and qualitative numerical experiments reveal the capability of gradients estimated by regression trees to improve predictive analysis, solve tasks in uncertainty quantification, and provide interpretation of model behavior.
